overview: Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust is a London-listed, closed-end investment trust managed by Baillie Gifford that aims to identify, own and support the world's most exceptional growth companies across both public and private markets globally. It is not an operating company but a permanent-capital vehicle holding a concentrated, high-conviction portfolio (roughly 80 public and 50-plus private positions) with a long (5-10+ year) holding horizon, benchmarked against the FTSE All-World Index. Fiscal year end is 31 March; the trust has traded on the London Stock Exchange since 1909 and is a FTSE 100 constituent.

business_model.summary: SMT generates shareholder returns from capital appreciation of a concentrated global equity portfolio (public and private), financed by permanent share capital plus modest structural gearing (borrowings). Baillie Gifford & Co is sole manager and AIFM, charging a low, tiered ad valorem management fee with no performance fee (ongoing charges ~0.33% in FY2026, among the lowest of any actively managed global or private-equity-adjacent vehicle). As a closed-end structure, the trust does not have to sell holdings to meet redemptions, allowing it to hold illiquid private companies through their full growth cycle, including into and beyond an eventual public listing (e.g. SpaceX IPO, June 2026).

revenue_streams.name: Capital gains on public equity holdings
Capital gains on private/unlisted company holdings

business_model.customer_type: Retail and institutional shareholders (UK-focused but increasingly international); the trust itself is a wholesale allocator of capital to growth companies, public and private, globally
business_model.geographic_mix: Portfolio: USA ~60%, China ~14%, Taiwan ~6%, Brazil ~6-7%, Netherlands ~5%, Sweden/Singapore/Korea/Germany smaller weights; listed on LSE, reports in GBP

main_competitors: Open-ended global growth funds (e.g. Baillie Gifford Long Term Global Growth, Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price Global growth funds)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest and most prominent generalist global growth trusts in the UK, and historically the most popular investment trust by retail flows; distinctive for genuinely large (c.20%), long-dated private-company exposure others cannot replicate at this scale and liquidity

moat_factors.description: Long relationships and reputation as a patient, non-time-limited investor give Baillie Gifford access to late-stage private rounds (SpaceX, Anthropic, ByteDance, Stripe, Databricks) that most listed funds and even many private equity vehicles cannot obtain
Unlike open-ended funds, SMT is never forced to sell into weakness to meet redemptions, enabling it to hold through volatility and private-to-public transitions (e.g. SpaceX IPO lock-up)
Ongoing charges ~0.33% with no performance fee is far below typical private equity/venture fee structures (2-and-20) and below most active public equity peers
FTSE 100-sized trust offers daily liquid access to a basket that includes illiquid private names, a structural advantage versus direct private equity funds

Baillie Gifford's 118-year-old partnership culture and long-only, patient-capital philosophy is well regarded, though recent 5-year NAV returns (12.8% over 5 years, versus 68.2% for FTSE All-World) show the moat has not translated into consistent outperformance

weaknesses: Heavy dependence on a small number of mega-positions (SpaceX alone ~19-26% of assets) for performance
Discount to NAV has been structurally persistent (c.9-10% through FY2025-26, briefly moving to a small premium post year-end) despite large buybacks
Five-year NAV total return (12.8%) has lagged the FTSE All-World Index (68.2%) materially, a legacy of the 2021-2022 growth/rate-driven drawdown
Private company valuations are marked by the manager/board rather than a public market, inviting scepticism during periods of volatility
Historically close association with a small number of highly visible, often controversial, founder-led companies (Tesla/Musk, formerly)

growth_drivers: AI infrastructure buildout thesis across the stack: chips/foundry (NVIDIA, TSMC, ASML), compute/cloud, foundation models (Anthropic, MiniMax) and application layers
SpaceX's Starlink direct-to-phone expansion, Golden Dome defense contracts, and potential orbital AI compute/data centre economics
Realisation events as large private holdings move toward public listings (SpaceX completed IPO June 2026 at $135/share; ByteDance, Anthropic, Stripe, Databricks flagged as future listing candidates)
Expanded private-company investment capacity: shareholders approved (10 April 2026) an additional £250m of headroom above the 30% private-company limit, subject to annual renewal
Continued share buybacks shrinking share count and (management argues) narrowing the discount over time
Selective exposure to Chinese AI/platform ecosystem (ByteDance, MiniMax, RedNote, CATL) as a differentiated, lower-priced way to access AI/EV supply chain winners
Secular themes beyond AI: digitalisation of finance (MercadoLibre, Nubank, Stripe, Revolut), autonomous transport (Joby, Aurora, Zipline), and healthcare/genomics innovation (Moderna, Tempus AI)

business.description: SpaceX reached roughly 19-26% of total assets in FY2026, a degree of concentration the managers themselves call 'highly unusual'; a reversal in SpaceX's valuation, a Starship failure, or adverse regulatory action would have an outsized portfolio impact

~20% of the portfolio (c.50 private companies) is valued by the manager/board using modelled and comparable-based fair value rather than observable market prices; valuations can move sharply (average top-10 private position revaluation +86% in FY2026) and are inherently harder to verify or to exit at stated value

business.risk: Sector/style concentration in growth and technology
business.description: Technology is ~43% of the portfolio versus ~31% for the FTSE All-World Index, and software/AI-exposed names have seen sharp valuation compression (global software sector down roughly $2tn in market cap over the past year per the FY2026 manager review)

business.risk: China exposure amid weak domestic demand and price wars
business.description: Meituan swung to an operating loss amid a food-delivery price war with Alibaba/JD.com; broader 'involution' dynamics are compressing margins across Chinese industries the trust is exposed to (e.g. EV battery/solar manufacturing, e-commerce)
Full exit from Tesla in FY2026 after a multi-year reduction shows thesis risk even in long-held, high-conviction positions

financial.description: The trust borrows to invest (gross/net gearing ~8% mid-2026, having been ~11-13% at recent fiscal year-ends); gearing amplifies both gains and losses, and a fall in portfolio value increases the proportional loss to equity holders
Shares can trade at a material discount or premium to NAV; buying at a premium or selling into a widening discount can impair shareholder returns independent of underlying portfolio performance
The great majority of holdings are denominated in USD and other non-GBP currencies (portfolio ~60% US, with Taiwan, China, Brazil, Europe exposure) against a GBP-reporting, GBP-share-priced trust

Average cost of debt is low (~3.6% in FY2026, ~3.1% in FY2025) following periodic refinancing of bank facilities and loan notes, but a sustained rise in rates would raise the cost of maintained gearing

regulatory.description: Baillie Gifford is the regulated AIFM; the trust itself is a UK-listed company not directly FCA-regulated, but is subject to AIC/LSE listing rules and periodic UK retail-disclosure regime changes (e.g. cost-disclosure rules affecting investment trust comparability)

regulatory.risk: Shareholder approval constraints on private allocation
regulatory.description: The 30% private-company limit (plus a new conditional £250m/annual-renewal buffer) constrains the pace of private investment and requires recurring shareholder votes

regulatory.risk: Geopolitical/trade policy shocks to portfolio companies
regulatory.description: US tariff actions, China trade retaliation, and conflict-driven disruption (e.g. Strait of Hormuz closure cited in FY2026 report) directly affected cross-border commerce holdings (PDD/Temu, Sea Limited, Adyen, Wayfair)

macro.risk: Interest rate sensitivity of long-duration growth equities
macro.description: As a portfolio of long-duration growth and often pre-profit companies, NAV is sensitive to discount-rate/interest-rate moves; the 2021-22 rate-hiking cycle drove the trust's weak 5-year NAV record (12.8%) relative to the index

Managers note fundamental investors are under 15% of US equity trading volume, with short-horizon, leveraged participants driving outsized single-day moves (e.g. 20-30% swings in March 2026) unrelated to company fundamentals

macro.risk: AI capex cycle moderation or overbuild/bust
macro.description: Managers explicitly flag historical precedent (railways, canals, fibre-optic buildout) for technology cycles ending in financial overshoot even where the underlying technology proves transformational

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global growth-equity/AI-infrastructure investment theme remains a dominant driver; AIC-sector-wide headwinds persist for UK investment trusts generally (discounts, subdued retail demand for the wrapper), though SMT has outperformed the AIC Global sector average on both NAV and share price in FY2026
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — portfolio skewed to long-duration growth, early/late-stage private companies and technology/AI capex, all of which are sensitive to the economic and rate cycle; trust-level discount/premium adds a second, sentiment-driven layer of cyclicality on top of NAV
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — both because of long-duration growth-equity valuations (discount-rate sensitive) and because the trust itself uses geared borrowing (~8-13% gearing)
macro_factors.currency_exposure: High — majority of underlying holdings are USD (and other non-GBP) denominated against a GBP-reporting trust; FX moves affect reported NAV
key_input_costs: Cost of borrowing/gearing (average ~3.1-3.6% in recent years)

recent_developments.event: Shareholders approved (99.7% in favour) a change to investment policy granting up to an additional £250m of private-company investment capacity above the existing 30% limit, subject to annual renewal

SpaceX completed its long-anticipated IPO at $135/share, listing on a US exchange; SMT and other existing holders are subject to a post-IPO lock-up. SpaceX was over 19-25% of trust assets at various points in 2026, by far the largest single contributor to FY2026 performance
NAV total return of 27.4% and share price total return of 26.8%, both well ahead of the FTSE All-World Index's 18.0%; 10-year NAV total return of 435.2% versus 233.9% for the index

Full exit from Tesla, citing intensifying EV competition (especially in China) and valuation that already prices in optionality from autonomy/robotics; new positions initiated in EQT Corporation and Vistra Energy (US natural gas and nuclear/gas power generation serving AI data-centre demand), plus Anthropic, CATL, RedNote, MiniMax and Figma

Discount to NAV widened modestly from ~9.0% (March 2025) to ~9.5% (March 2026) despite continued large-scale buybacks; company noted the year-end discount was distorted by a sharp final-day NAV move, and that post year-end the shares moved to trade at a modest premium, prompting share issuance in line with policy
Gearing eased from ~13% to ~11% at fiscal year-end (further down to ~8% by mid-2026) as portfolio growth outpaced absolute borrowings; average cost of debt ~3.6%

Dividend increased 4.3% to 4.57p per share, extending the trust's 43-consecutive-year dividend growth record (AIC 'Dividend Hero'), despite the portfolio being managed for capital growth rather than income

Board changes: Heather Manners joined the Board; Professor Patrick Maxwell announced his retirement, with Sharon Flood succeeding him as Senior Independent Director and chairing a newly established Remuneration Committee

Manager commentary (Lawrence Burns) suggested the trust may be under-exposed to AI rather than over-exposed, and that renewed private-company buying (ByteDance, Stripe, Databricks) resumed once SpaceX's IPO freed headroom under the 30% private-asset cap

Continued large-scale share buybacks (hundreds of millions of pounds per year, following the board's March 2024 commitment of at least £1bn over two years) have materially shrunk the share count, a structural response to the persistent discount

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Report (year to 31 March 2026), published May 2026

items.period: FY2026 actual, expected to remain low going forward
items.notes: No performance fee; Board and Managers reiterate a structural commitment to keeping costs low as a core proposition versus both active public equity funds and private equity vehicles

items.target: Managed dynamically as a 'long-term tool to enhance returns, used judiciously' — no fixed target range disclosed, but gearing has been run in the roughly 8-13% band over FY2025-26
items.vs_prior: declining (13% -> 11% at FY2026 year end -> ~8% by mid-2026)
items.notes: Reduction reflects portfolio NAV growth outpacing absolute borrowings, not active deleveraging

items.target: 30% of total assets at time of purchase, plus an additional conditional £250m headroom approved April 2026 (subject to annual shareholder renewal)
items.notes: Portfolio was at/above the 30% threshold for periods of FY2026 due to SpaceX's appreciation; SpaceX's IPO completion (June 2026) mechanically reduces the 'private' designation of that position going forward

items.target: Continue buybacks 'should the shares return to trading at a discount'
items.notes: Policy-based rather than a fixed £ target for FY2027; post year-end the trust briefly moved to a premium, triggering share issuance instead of buybacks in line with stated policy

items.target: 4.57p per share for FY2026 (final dividend 2.97p, paid 10 July 2026); continuation of long-term growth expected
items.notes: Dividend is a by-product of modest portfolio income, not a primary investment objective; trust remains an AIC 'Dividend Hero' with 43 consecutive years of increases

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Christopher Samuel reiterated that the Board judges performance over multi-year, not single-year, periods, and that the discount at FY2026 year-end was distorted by a sharp final-day NAV move. Managers Tom Slater and Lawrence Burns framed FY2026 around two interlocking forces: an accelerating AI infrastructure buildout (viewed as a once-in-a-generation structural shift, with SpaceX, Anthropic, TSMC, ASML and NVIDIA as key beneficiaries) and a 'fracturing' of the post-war trade/geopolitical order that directly hurt certain holdings (PDD/Temu, Sea Limited, Adyen, Hermès, Ferrari, Meituan). Slater explicitly flagged SpaceX's size (~19%+ of assets at year end) as 'highly unusual' concentration and a source of potential volatility, while defending the trust's willingness to hold such positions as central to its reason for existing. Burns separately suggested in press commentary mid-2026 that the bigger risk may be under-exposure rather than over-exposure to AI.

bull_case: Unique structural access to the world's most valuable private AI/tech companies (SpaceX, Anthropic, ByteDance, Stripe, Databricks) at scale and with daily liquidity that no comparable listed vehicle offers

Strong recent absolute and relative performance — FY2026 NAV total return of 27.4% versus 18.0% for the FTSE All-World Index, and a 10-year NAV return of 435.2% versus 233.9% for the index — reasserting the long-term case after a weak 2021-2023 stretch

Persistent discount to NAV (c.9-10% through most of FY2026) combined with an active, well-funded buyback programme offers a potential value-realisation catalyst if the discount narrows, as already glimpsed in the brief post-year-end move to a premium

Very low ongoing charges (~0.33%, no performance fee) relative to both actively managed public equity peers and private equity/venture alternatives, meaning shareholders keep more of any gross return generated
Direct, differentiated exposure to the AI infrastructure buildout across the value chain (compute, chips, foundation models, power) at a point management believes is still in its early stages
bear_case: Extreme concentration risk: SpaceX alone reached ~19-26% of total assets in FY2026; any setback (Starship failure, regulatory action, valuation reset post-lock-up) would disproportionately hit NAV

Private holdings (~20% of the portfolio, c.50 companies) are valued using manager/board judgment rather than observable market prices, creating valuation uncertainty and potential for sharp mark-downs in a risk-off environment

Structural, geared, growth/tech-tilted portfolio is highly sensitive to interest rates and risk sentiment; the trust's weak 5-year NAV return (12.8% versus 68.2% for the index) shows how badly this can underperform in an unfavourable rate/valuation cycle

The discount to NAV has proven persistent despite years of large-scale buybacks (moving from ~9.0% to ~9.5% over FY2026 before a brief post-year-end premium), suggesting structural demand weakness for the trust/sector that buybacks alone may not resolve

Heavy China exposure (~14% of the portfolio) sits in sectors experiencing margin-destructive price wars ('involution') and is vulnerable to further US-China trade/tariff escalation, as seen in FY2026 with PDD/Temu, Sea Limited and Meituan
